stem: You want to find security vulnerabilities in your own source code by analyzing how untrusted data flows through the application, before the code ever runs. Which GitHub Advanced Security feature and engine does this?

options.text: Code scanning powered by CodeQL, which runs static analysis by querying a database it builds from your code
Secret scanning, which matches committed strings against known credential patterns
Dependabot, which compares your manifest against an advisory database
Required status checks, which block a merge until tests pass

explanationCorrect: Code scanning uses CodeQL to treat your code as data: it builds a database from the code and runs queries that trace tainted data from a source to a dangerous sink, so it finds issues by static analysis without executing anything.
explanationIncorrect: Secret scanning looks for credentials that were committed, matching strings against known token patterns; it does not reason about data flow through your code. Dependabot works at the dependency level, comparing the versions in your manifests and lockfiles against the GitHub Advisory Database, so it flags vulnerable packages you depend on rather than flaws in code you wrote. Required status checks are a branch protection mechanism that gates merges on CI results; they run whatever you configured but do no security analysis themselves. The feature that performs data-flow static analysis of your own source is code scanning with CodeQL.

stem: A developer is about to commit an AWS access key. You want GitHub to block the push at the moment it is attempted, before the secret ever reaches the remote repository. Which capability do you enable?

options.text: Secret scanning push protection
Branch protection requiring a pull request review
Code scanning with a custom CodeQL query that looks for secrets
Dependabot security updates

explanationCorrect: Push protection is the part of secret scanning that checks the pushed content against supported secret patterns and rejects the push in real time, so a recognized credential never lands in the remote history in the first place.
explanationIncorrect: A pull request review requirement gates merging into a protected branch, but the secret would already be pushed to the feature branch and stored in history before any review happens, so it does not prevent the leak. CodeQL analyzes code structure and data flow rather than scanning for credential patterns, and it runs as an analysis over a branch rather than as a gate on the push itself. Dependabot security updates open pull requests to bump vulnerable dependencies and have nothing to do with committed secrets. The feature that stops a recognized secret at push time is secret scanning push protection.

stem: When a new advisory affects a package your repository depends on, you want Dependabot to automatically open a pull request that bumps that dependency to a patched version. Which Dependabot feature is this?

options.text: Dependabot security updates
Dependabot version updates
Dependabot alerts
Dependency review in a pull request

explanationCorrect: Dependabot security updates react specifically to advisories: when a vulnerability is known for a dependency you use, Dependabot raises a pull request to move it to the nearest patched version.
explanationIncorrect: Dependabot version updates are scheduled and driven by a dependabot.yml config; they keep dependencies current on a cadence regardless of whether a vulnerability exists, so they are not triggered by an advisory. Dependabot alerts notify you that a vulnerable dependency is present, but an alert on its own is a notification, not an automatically opened fix pull request. Dependency review runs in a pull request and shows the security impact of the dependency changes that pull request introduces, helping a reviewer decide before merge; it does not itself open remediation pull requests. The feature that opens patch pull requests in response to advisories is Dependabot security updates.

stem: As an organization owner you want a single place to see which repositories have open code scanning, secret scanning, and Dependabot alerts across the whole organization, and where those features are enabled. Where do you look?

options.text: The organization-level security overview
The Insights tab of each repository, one repository at a time
The Actions tab filtered by workflow run
A CSV export of the git commit log

explanationCorrect: The security overview aggregates alert state and feature enablement across the organization's repositories in one view, which is exactly the cross-repository posture picture an owner needs.
explanationIncorrect: The repository Insights tab shows traffic and contribution analytics for a single repository and does not aggregate security alerts across the org, so using it means visiting every repository by hand. The Actions tab lists workflow runs; it can tell you whether a scanning workflow executed but not the consolidated alert posture across repositories. A commit log export tells you what changed, not which security alerts are open or which features are turned on. The consolidated cross-repository view is the organization-level security overview.

stem: You need to customize which CodeQL query suites run and add a build step for a compiled language before analysis. Which code scanning configuration should you use?

options.text: Advanced setup, which commits an editable CodeQL analysis workflow you can customize
Default setup, because its managed configuration can be edited per query and per build step
Secret scanning custom patterns
A branch protection rule that adds the build step

explanationCorrect: Advanced setup generates a CodeQL workflow file in your repository that you own and edit, so you can choose query suites, set languages, and insert build steps for compiled languages that need to be built before CodeQL can analyze them.
explanationIncorrect: Default setup is deliberately managed and low-configuration: it enables code scanning quickly and handles common cases, but it does not give you a workflow file to hand-tune query suites or inject a custom build step, which is the whole requirement here. Secret scanning custom patterns define new credential shapes to detect; they are unrelated to CodeQL queries or building code. A branch protection rule can require the code scanning check to pass, but it cannot define how the analysis runs or add a build step. To customize query suites and add a build step you use advanced setup with its editable CodeQL workflow.

stem: You want scheduled version updates for your npm dependencies. What is the minimum you configure, and where?

options.text: A .github/dependabot.yml with an updates entry specifying package-ecosystem, directory, and schedule.interval
A workflow that runs npm update on a cron schedule
Enable Dependabot alerts and nothing else
A CODEOWNERS entry that lists package.json

explanationCorrect: Dependabot version updates are driven by .github/dependabot.yml, where each updates entry names the package-ecosystem (npm), the directory of the manifest, and a schedule.interval, which together tell Dependabot what to keep current and how often.
explanationIncorrect: Running npm update on a cron would change the lockfile but produces no reviewed pull requests and is not how Dependabot version updates work. Enabling alerts only tells you about known vulnerabilities; it does not open routine version-bump pull requests. CODEOWNERS assigns review responsibility and does nothing to schedule updates. The minimum for version updates is a dependabot.yml updates entry with ecosystem, directory, and interval.

stem: Dependabot alerts tell you a dependency you use is vulnerable. Where does that vulnerability information primarily come from?

options.text: The GitHub Advisory Database, matched against your repository's dependency graph
CodeQL query results over your source code
Secret scanning credential patterns
A one-time npm audit run on your laptop

explanationCorrect: Dependabot compares the packages in your dependency graph against advisories in the GitHub Advisory Database, and raises an alert when a version you depend on is covered by a known vulnerability.
explanationIncorrect: CodeQL analyzes your own source for flaws; it does not track third-party package advisories. Secret scanning looks for leaked credentials, not vulnerable dependencies. A local npm audit is a manual, point-in-time check that is not what powers continuous Dependabot alerts in GitHub. The source is the GitHub Advisory Database applied to your dependency graph.

stem: Dependabot alerts and security updates are not appearing for a repository. Which prerequisite feature must be enabled for them to function?

options.text: The dependency graph
GitHub Pages
Repository Discussions
A self-hosted runner

explanationCorrect: The dependency graph is what identifies the packages a repository uses; Dependabot alerts and security updates build on it, so they cannot work until the dependency graph is enabled.
explanationIncorrect: GitHub Pages publishes a website and is unrelated to dependency analysis. Discussions is a community forum feature with no bearing on Dependabot. A self-hosted runner executes workflow jobs; Dependabot's alerting does not depend on your runners. The required foundation is the dependency graph.

stem: You want a pull request to fail before merge if it introduces a dependency with a known high-severity vulnerability. Which mechanism does this?

options.text: The dependency review action running on pull_request, configured to fail on a severity threshold and set as a required check
Dependabot version updates on a weekly schedule
Secret scanning push protection
CodeQL default setup analyzing the diff

explanationCorrect: The dependency review action inspects the dependency changes a pull request introduces and can fail the check when a new dependency meets or exceeds a configured severity, and making it a required check blocks the merge.
explanationIncorrect: Dependabot version updates open bump pull requests on a schedule; they do not gate other people's pull requests on newly introduced vulnerabilities. Secret scanning push protection blocks committed credentials, not vulnerable dependencies. CodeQL analyzes source code for code-level flaws, not the security of dependencies a pull request adds. The gate for newly introduced vulnerable dependencies is the dependency review action as a required check.

stem: Dependabot is opening too many individual version-update pull requests. How do you make it combine related updates into fewer pull requests?

options.text: Configure groups in dependabot.yml so related updates are batched into a single pull request
Set schedule.interval to monthly, which automatically merges the pull requests
Disable Dependabot alerts to reduce the noise
Set open-pull-requests-limit to 1 so updates are combined

explanationCorrect: The groups setting in dependabot.yml tells Dependabot to bundle updates that match a group into one pull request, which is the intended way to cut down on the number of separate update PRs.
explanationIncorrect: Changing the interval to monthly only changes how often updates run; it does not merge multiple updates into one pull request. Disabling alerts hides vulnerability information and does not affect version-update pull request volume. open-pull-requests-limit caps how many update PRs are open at once and simply drops the rest; it does not combine them into one. The batching feature is groups.

stem: A specific package must not be bumped past its current major version because the next major has breaking changes. How do you express that to Dependabot?

options.text: Add an ignore entry for that dependency in dependabot.yml constraining the versions or update-types it may propose
Remove the package from the dependency graph
Add the package to .gitignore
Turn off Dependabot entirely for the repository

explanationCorrect: dependabot.yml supports an ignore list where you name a dependency and restrict which versions or update-types Dependabot may raise, so you can block the major bump while still receiving patch and minor updates.
explanationIncorrect: You cannot selectively remove a real dependency from the graph while still using it; the graph reflects your manifests. .gitignore excludes files from version control and has no effect on Dependabot. Disabling Dependabot entirely throws away all updates, including the safe ones you still want. The targeted control is an ignore entry with version or update-type constraints.

stem: Beyond vulnerabilities, you also need pull requests to fail when they introduce a dependency under a license your organization disallows. Can the dependency review action enforce this?

options.text: Yes; the dependency review action supports allow and deny license configuration and can fail on a disallowed license
No; license policy requires a separate paid third-party tool
No; only CodeQL can evaluate dependency licenses
No; license information is only exposed through secret scanning

explanationCorrect: The dependency review action can be configured with license allow or deny lists, so a pull request that adds a dependency under a denied license fails the check, giving you license policy enforcement alongside vulnerability checks.
explanationIncorrect: License enforcement is built into the dependency review action, so a separate paid tool is not required. CodeQL analyzes source code for flaws and does not evaluate dependency licenses. Secret scanning finds leaked credentials and has nothing to do with license metadata. The dependency review action itself handles license allow and deny policy.

stem: Some of your dependencies come from a private package registry that requires authentication. How does Dependabot reach it securely?

options.text: Declare a registries block in dependabot.yml and reference Dependabot secrets for the credentials
Put the registry password in plaintext directly in dependabot.yml
Dependabot cannot authenticate to private registries at all
Commit an .npmrc containing the token into the repository

explanationCorrect: dependabot.yml has a registries section for private sources, and credentials are supplied through Dependabot secrets referenced from that section, so Dependabot can authenticate without exposing the secret in the config.
explanationIncorrect: A plaintext password in the config would be committed to the repository and leaked, which is exactly what Dependabot secrets exist to avoid. Dependabot does support private registries, so claiming it cannot is wrong. Committing an .npmrc with a live token is the same plaintext-secret leak in a different file. The secure pattern is a registries block referencing Dependabot secrets.

stem: A Dependabot security update opens a pull request for a vulnerable dependency. To which version does it typically bump the dependency?

options.text: The minimum version that resolves the advisory, to limit unrelated change
Always the newest available major version
The oldest version still in the registry
It removes the dependency from the manifest

explanationCorrect: A security update aims to fix the vulnerability with the smallest necessary change, bumping to the lowest version that is no longer affected, which keeps the pull request low-risk and easy to review.
explanationIncorrect: Jumping to the newest major version would often introduce breaking changes unrelated to the fix, which is not what a security update targets. The oldest version would not resolve the advisory and may itself be vulnerable. Dependabot does not delete a dependency you rely on; it patches it. The behavior is to move to the minimum patched version.

stem: An auditor asks for a machine-readable inventory of every dependency your repository uses. Which capability produces that inventory?

options.text: Export an SBOM in SPDX format from the repository's dependency graph
Download the CodeQL database for the repository
Export the list of secret scanning alerts
Save the workflow run logs from the Actions tab

explanationCorrect: The dependency graph can be exported as a Software Bill of Materials in SPDX format, which is exactly the standardized, machine-readable dependency inventory an auditor is asking for.
explanationIncorrect: A CodeQL database is an analysis artifact of your source code, not a dependency inventory. Secret scanning alerts list leaked credentials, not dependencies. Workflow run logs record what a job did, not a structured list of the packages you depend on. The SBOM export from the dependency graph is the right artifact.

stem: You run a third-party static analysis tool and want its findings to show up in GitHub's code scanning alerts. What format must the tool emit, and how does GitHub ingest it?

options.text: Emit SARIF and upload it to code scanning via the upload-sarif action or the API
Emit JUnit XML and attach it as a build artifact
Emit a CodeQL database for GitHub to query
Print the findings to the workflow job log

explanationCorrect: Code scanning ingests results in SARIF, the standard static-analysis interchange format, so a third-party tool that outputs SARIF can be uploaded (with the upload-sarif action or API) and its findings appear alongside CodeQL alerts.
explanationIncorrect: JUnit XML describes test results, not security findings, and code scanning does not consume it. A CodeQL database is an internal analysis artifact CodeQL builds from source; a third-party tool does not produce one, and it is not how external results are uploaded. Printing to the log leaves the findings unstructured and unlinked to the Security tab. The interchange format for code scanning is SARIF.

stem: You want code scanning to include additional code-quality queries alongside the security queries. Which CodeQL query suite do you select?

options.text: The security-and-quality suite
The security-extended suite
The default suite
There is no suite that includes quality queries

explanationCorrect: The security-and-quality suite runs the security queries plus additional maintainability and quality queries, which is what you choose when you want both categories.
explanationIncorrect: security-extended broadens the security coverage with more security queries but does not add code-quality queries. The default suite is the smaller, high-precision security set and includes the fewest queries. Quality queries do exist as a suite, so the claim that none includes them is wrong. The suite that adds quality queries is security-and-quality.

stem: Scanning a Java project with CodeQL requires the code to be built so CodeQL can observe compilation. How does CodeQL handle the build?

options.text: It runs an autobuild step that attempts the build automatically, and you can supply manual build commands if autobuild fails
CodeQL never needs to build code for any language
Dependabot compiles the project for CodeQL
The runner refuses to analyze compiled languages

explanationCorrect: For compiled languages CodeQL uses autobuild to try to build the project automatically, and when autobuild cannot figure out the build you replace it with explicit build commands so CodeQL can trace the compilation.
explanationIncorrect: Interpreted languages need no build, but compiled languages like Java do, so the claim that CodeQL never builds is false. Dependabot manages dependencies and does not build code for CodeQL. Compiled languages are fully supported, so the runner does not refuse them. The mechanism is autobuild, with manual build steps as a fallback.

stem: Which statement about CodeQL language support is accurate?

options.text: CodeQL supports a defined set of compiled and interpreted languages, and code in unsupported languages is simply not analyzed
CodeQL analyzes every programming language that exists
CodeQL supports only JavaScript
CodeQL supports only compiled languages

explanationCorrect: CodeQL covers a specific list of supported languages spanning both compiled and interpreted ones (such as Java, C/C++, C#, Go, JavaScript/TypeScript, Python, Ruby, and Swift); anything outside that list is not analyzed rather than analyzed poorly.
explanationIncorrect: No analyzer supports every language in existence, so that claim is false. CodeQL supports far more than JavaScript alone. It supports interpreted languages as well as compiled ones, so restricting it to compiled languages is wrong. The accurate description is a defined set of supported languages, with unsupported code left unanalyzed.

stem: A code scanning alert is a confirmed false positive. How should you handle it so it stops recurring while keeping an audit trail?

options.text: Dismiss the alert with a reason such as false positive, which records who dismissed it and why
Delete the source file that triggered it
Disable code scanning for the whole repository
Do nothing, since alerts expire automatically

explanationCorrect: Dismissing an alert with a documented reason (false positive, used in tests, or won't fix) clears it from the active list, keeps it from recurring for the same finding, and records the actor and rationale for audit.
explanationIncorrect: Deleting the source file to silence an alert is destructive and usually wrong; the code may be needed. Disabling code scanning entirely removes coverage for every real issue, not just the false positive. Alerts do not silently expire; leaving it open keeps noise and hides real signal. The correct action is a documented dismissal.

stem: Code scanning runs on a pull request and finds a new problem introduced by that pull request. Where does the developer see it?

options.text: As a check on the pull request with inline annotations, and in the repository's Security tab under code scanning alerts
Only in a nightly summary email
Only buried in the Actions run logs
In the repository Wiki

explanationCorrect: Code scanning surfaces pull request findings as a check with inline annotations on the changed lines, and all alerts are also collected in the Security tab, so developers see issues right where they are working.
explanationIncorrect: Findings are shown in real time on the pull request, not only in a nightly email. They are more than log lines; they are structured alerts with locations, so the Actions log is not where you triage them. The Wiki is unrelated documentation space. Results appear on the pull request check and in the Security tab.

stem: Your security team wrote custom CodeQL queries to catch a framework-specific bug pattern. How do you run them in code scanning?

options.text: Package them as a CodeQL query pack (or reference the .ql files) and point the code scanning workflow's queries input at them
Paste them into the secret scanning custom patterns UI
Add them to dependabot.yml as an updates entry
Custom CodeQL queries cannot be run in code scanning

explanationCorrect: Custom queries are distributed as CodeQL query packs (or referenced directly), and the code scanning workflow's queries input tells CodeQL to run them in addition to or instead of the standard suites.
explanationIncorrect: Secret scanning custom patterns are regexes for credentials, not CodeQL queries. dependabot.yml configures dependency updates and cannot run analysis queries. Custom queries are explicitly supported, so claiming they cannot run is wrong. You run them by packaging a query pack and referencing it from the queries input.

stem: Your company issues an internal API token with a distinctive format that GitHub does not detect out of the box. How do you get secret scanning to catch it?

options.text: Define a custom secret scanning pattern with a regular expression at the repository, organization, or enterprise level
Add the token format to your CodeQL query suite
List the token format in dependabot.yml
Nothing can be done; only GitHub partner patterns are detectable

explanationCorrect: Custom patterns let you describe an organization-specific secret with a regular expression so secret scanning detects it just like a built-in pattern, at whichever scope you define it.
explanationIncorrect: CodeQL analyzes code logic and data flow, not credential string shapes, so a token format does not belong in a query suite. dependabot.yml configures dependency updates and cannot define secret patterns. Secret scanning is not limited to partner patterns; custom patterns are exactly the extension point for internal formats. The answer is a custom secret scanning pattern.

stem: Secret scanning detects a real cloud-provider key that leaked in a public repository. Through GitHub's partner program, what can happen automatically?

options.text: GitHub notifies the provider, who may automatically revoke or rotate the exposed credential
GitHub emails all of your customers about the leak
The repository is automatically deleted
Nothing happens unless you open a support ticket

explanationCorrect: For public repositories, GitHub participates in a partner program: when a supported provider's secret is detected, GitHub notifies that provider, who can revoke or rotate the credential to limit the damage.
explanationIncorrect: GitHub does not email your customers; the notification goes to the credential's provider. It does not delete your repository. And the partner notification is automatic for supported secrets, so it does not wait on a support ticket. The automatic action is provider notification and possible revocation.

stem: Push protection blocks a commit, but the developer determines the flagged string is a harmless test placeholder. What is the intended way forward?

options.text: Allow the push by supplying a bypass reason such as false positive or used in tests, which is recorded for auditing
Force-push to a brand new branch to slip past the check
Delete and recreate the repository
Permanently disable secret scanning for everyone

explanationCorrect: Push protection lets an author bypass the block by selecting a reason, and that bypass is logged, so a genuine false positive can proceed while security teams retain an audit trail of who allowed it and why.
explanationIncorrect: Trying to force-push around the control is an evasion, not the intended workflow, and push protection still applies. Recreating the repository is drastic and pointless. Disabling secret scanning removes protection for everyone to resolve one placeholder. The intended path is a documented push-protection bypass.

stem: You just enabled secret scanning on an existing repository with years of commit history. Does it look only at new commits going forward?

options.text: No; secret scanning also scans the repository's full existing git history for known secret patterns
Yes; only commits made after enablement are ever scanned
It scans only the latest commit on the default branch
It scans only currently open pull requests

explanationCorrect: When enabled, secret scanning scans the entire repository history, not just future commits, so a secret committed long ago is still surfaced as an alert.
explanationIncorrect: Limiting to post-enablement commits would miss the many secrets already sitting in history, which is not how it works. Scanning only the latest commit or only open pull requests would likewise miss historical leaks. Secret scanning covers the full git history.

stem: A directory of test fixtures contains deliberately fake tokens that keep raising secret scanning alerts. How do you stop alerts for that path without weakening scanning elsewhere?

options.text: Configure paths to exclude for secret scanning (a secret_scanning.yml paths-ignore entry)
Add the directory to .gitignore
Delete the fixtures directory
Turn secret scanning off for the whole repository

explanationCorrect: Secret scanning supports excluding specific paths through its configuration (paths-ignore), so you can silence alerts on a known-fake fixtures directory while keeping full scanning on the rest of the repository.
explanationIncorrect: .gitignore only prevents files from being tracked; files already committed are still scanned, and you likely need the fixtures committed. Deleting the fixtures removes test data you rely on. Disabling scanning repository-wide removes protection everywhere to fix one directory. The precise control is a paths exclusion.

stem: For supported providers, secret scanning can tell you whether a detected token is still usable right now. What is this capability called?

options.text: Validity checks (secret validation), which query the provider to report the secret as active or inactive
CodeQL data-flow analysis of the token
Dependency review of the token
Push protection

explanationCorrect: Validity checks ask the provider whether a detected secret is still active, so responders can prioritize a live, exploitable credential over one that has already been revoked.
explanationIncorrect: CodeQL data-flow analysis reasons about code, not whether a credential is currently valid at its provider. Dependency review evaluates dependency changes in pull requests. Push protection blocks new secrets at push time; it does not report the live status of an already-detected one. The status feature is validity checks.

stem: For public repositories on GitHub.com, which of these security capabilities are available at no cost?

options.text: Code scanning, secret scanning, and dependency review are available free on public repositories
None of them; every feature needs a paid license even on public repos
Only Dependabot alerts, and nothing else
They are free only for repositories owned by enterprise accounts

explanationCorrect: GitHub makes the core security features, including code scanning, secret scanning, and dependency review, available free for public repositories, which is why open-source projects can adopt them without a license.
explanationIncorrect: It is not the case that everything requires payment on public repos; the point of free public-repo access is broad open-source security. Access is not limited to Dependabot alerts alone. And it is not restricted to enterprise-owned repositories. On public repositories these features are free.

stem: You want code scanning and secret scanning enabled on your organization's private repositories. What is required?

options.text: A GitHub Advanced Security license (or the corresponding Code Security and Secret Protection products) for those private repositories
Nothing; the features are free on private repositories too
Only the free GitHub plan
A separate license for each self-hosted runner

explanationCorrect: On private repositories the advanced security features are paid: they require GitHub Advanced Security licensing (now also offered as the Code Security and Secret Protection products), unlike on public repositories where they are free.
explanationIncorrect: The features are not free on private repositories, which is the distinction from public ones. The free plan alone does not unlock them for private code. Runner licensing is unrelated to enabling these security features. Private repositories need GHAS (or Code Security / Secret Protection) licensing.

stem: GHAS can propose a concrete code fix directly on a code scanning alert to speed up remediation. What is this capability?

options.text: Copilot Autofix for code scanning, which suggests a fix for many CodeQL alerts
Dependabot security updates
Secret scanning push protection
A required status check

explanationCorrect: Copilot Autofix generates a suggested code change for many code scanning (CodeQL) alerts, so a developer can review and apply a fix inline instead of researching the remediation from scratch.
explanationIncorrect: Dependabot security updates fix vulnerable dependencies, not code-level alerts in your own source. Secret scanning push protection blocks committed secrets and does not propose code fixes. A required status check is a merge gate, not a fix suggestion. The suggested-fix feature for code scanning is Copilot Autofix.

stem: In a single repository, where do the code scanning, secret scanning, and Dependabot alerts all appear together?

options.text: The repository's Security tab
The Settings > Actions page
The repository Pulse view
A Projects board

explanationCorrect: The Security tab is the per-repository hub that collects code scanning, secret scanning, and Dependabot alerts, so responders have one place to review a repository's security posture.
explanationIncorrect: Settings > Actions configures workflow permissions and runners, not security alerts. Pulse summarizes recent repository activity like merged pull requests, not security findings. A Projects board tracks planned work items. The consolidated per-repo location is the Security tab.

stem: Which practice best embodies GHAS's prevention-first approach to secrets?

options.text: Enable push protection so secrets are blocked before they ever enter history, rather than only alerting after the fact
Rotate every secret once a year regardless of whether anything leaked
Wait for the partner program to revoke any leaked secrets for you
Rely solely on periodic manual code review to spot secrets

explanationCorrect: Prevention-first means stopping the problem at the source: push protection blocks a secret at push time so it never reaches the remote, which is far stronger than detecting and cleaning it up afterward.
explanationIncorrect: Scheduled rotation is good hygiene but is reactive and does nothing to stop a secret from being committed in the first place. Waiting on partner revocation is an after-the-fact safety net, not prevention, and only covers supported public-repo cases. Manual review is inconsistent and misses things at scale. The prevention-first control is push protection.

stem: You inherit hundreds of open security alerts and limited time. What is the most defensible way to prioritize remediation?

options.text: Prioritize by severity and exploitability or reachability, fixing high-severity, exploitable issues first
Fix alerts alphabetically by file name
Fix the oldest alerts first regardless of their severity
Dismiss all alerts to clear the backlog quickly

explanationCorrect: Risk-based prioritization focuses scarce effort where it matters: high-severity issues that are actually exploitable or reachable are fixed before low-impact ones, which reduces real risk fastest.
explanationIncorrect: Alphabetical order by file name has no relationship to risk. Oldest-first ignores that a newer critical vulnerability may be far more dangerous than an old low-severity one. Dismissing everything hides real risk and defeats the point of scanning. The defensible approach is to prioritize by severity and exploitability.

stem: To make security scanning consistently enforced rather than optional across many repositories, what is the recommended approach?

options.text: Enable the features at the organization level and require the relevant scans as status checks through branch protection or rulesets
Ask each developer to remember to run the scans locally
Enable scanning on a single flagship repository only
Review the Security tab manually once a quarter

explanationCorrect: Consistent enforcement comes from org-level enablement plus making the scans required checks via branch protection or rulesets, so pull requests cannot merge without passing and coverage does not depend on individual memory.
explanationIncorrect: Relying on developers to run scans locally is inconsistent and unauditable. Enabling scanning on one repository leaves the rest unprotected. A quarterly manual review is too infrequent to catch issues at merge time. Enforcement is achieved through org-wide enablement and required status checks.
